facts.fact: Makuhari Messe is a convention centre in Chiba City, just outside Tokyo, designed by Fumihiko Maki.
facts.quote: Makuhari Messe (幕張メッセ) is a convention center in Chiba City, Chiba Prefecture, Japan, located just outside of Tokyo. Designed by Fumihiko Maki, it is accessible by Tokyo's commuter rail system.

facts.fact: The name joins the area's name, Makuhari, with Messe, the German word for trade fair.
facts.quote: Makuhari is the name of the area, and Messe is a German language word meaning "trade fair".

facts.fact: The convention centre opened on 9 October 1989.
facts.quote: The convention center opened on 9 October 1989.

facts.fact: It was a venue for several sports at the Tokyo 2020 Olympic and Paralympic Games.
facts.quote: It was the venue for several sports during the Tokyo 2020 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

facts.fact: In 1994 the city of Vienna commissioned Zaha Hadid to design a three-part scheme to redevelop an area beside the Danube Canal.
facts.quote: In 1994, Hadid was commissioned by the city of Vienna to design and construct a three-part scheme for the urban redevelopment of an area adjacent to the Danube Canal.

facts.fact: The buildings stand along the Spittelauer Lände and cross over Otto Wagner's protected railway viaduct.
facts.quote: Situated along the Spittelauer Lände, the series of buildings interact with and cross over the railway viaduct by Viennese Modernist architect Otto Wagner, a protected structure.

facts.fact: The mixed-use scheme was described as a "sculpture-like overbuilding" of the historic Stadtbahn railway, and first had five buildings.
facts.quote: In its initial design consisting of five buildings, the mixed-use scheme, described as a "sculpture-like overbuilding" of the historic Stadtbahn railway, was designed by Hadid's practice ZHA.

facts.fact: Hadid and the artist Brian Clarke proposed glass mosaic and stained glass as part of the cladding and windows, but this was not built.
facts.quote: Hadid, together with British architectural artist Brian Clarke, developed an unexecuted collaborative proposal for the project that incorporated integral artworks by Clarke as part of the Neo-Futurist structures, with interrelated glass mosaic and traditionally-leaded stained glass forming part of the cladding and fenestration of the complex.

facts.fact: For the scheme Clarke developed a new mouth-blown glass he called 'Zaha-Glas'.
facts.quote: Clarke developed a new type of mouth-blown glass for the scheme, which he christened 'Zaha-Glas'.

facts.fact: Cut down to three buildings and delayed, the project was finished in 2006 without the artwork.
facts.quote: Later reduced to three buildings, the project, which experienced delays in construction, was completed in 2006, without the artwork.

facts.fact: The Teatre Nacional de Catalunya is a public theatre in Barcelona.
facts.quote: Teatre Nacional de Catalunya (TNC; Catalan pronunciation: [teˈatɾə nəsi.uˈnal də kətəˈluɲə]; National Theatre of Catalonia) is a public theatre located in Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain.

facts.fact: It stands on Plaça de les Arts, facing L'Auditori, near Plaça de les Glòries Catalanes.
facts.quote: The building is located at Plaça de les Arts, in front of L'Auditori and near Plaça de les Glòries Catalanes and is one of the emblematic cultural facilities of Barcelona.

facts.fact: Ricardo Bofill designed it as an ancient Greek temple, like some late 19th-century national theatres.
facts.quote: It was designed as an ancient Greek temple that resembled some other late 19th-century National Theatres by the prestigious Catalan postmodern architect Ricardo Bofill i Leví.

facts.fact: It was built from November 1991 to 1996.
facts.quote: Its construction took place from November 8, 1991, to 1996.

facts.fact: The design was controversial: some critics called it a parody or a mausoleum.
facts.quote: The result was polemic, and some detractors described it as a parody or as a mausoleum.

facts.fact: It has three halls: the Sala Gran with Greek-theatre seating for 866, the Sala Petita for 266 to 500, and the Sala Tallers, both with movable seating.
facts.quote: The facility shows three theatre halls suitable for performances: Sala Gran (in English: Big Hall), with a Greek theatre stands and capacity for 866 seats; Sala Petita (in English: Small Hall), with mobile stands and capacity between 266 and 500 people; and Sala Tallers (in English: Workshop Hall), with mobile stands.

facts.fact: It opened on 12 November 1996 with Tony Kushner's Angels in America.
facts.quote: On November 12, 1996, it opened with Àngels a Amèrica (Angels in America) by Tony Kushner, and directed by Josep Maria Flotats.

facts.fact: The House with Chimaeras is an Art Nouveau building in the Lypky neighbourhood of Kyiv.
facts.quote: House with Chimaeras (Ukrainian: Будинок з химерами, romanized: Budynok z khymeramy) or Horodetsky House (named for Władysław Horodecki) is an Art Nouveau building located in the historic Lypky neighborhood of Kyiv, the capital of Ukraine.

facts.fact: Władysław Horodecki built it in 1901–1902 as his own upmarket apartment building.
facts.quote: The Polish architect Władysław Horodecki originally constructed the House with Chimaeras for use as his own upmarket apartment building during 1901–1902.

facts.fact: Each floor was a single apartment, joined by a lift and stairs; Horodecki lived on the fourth floor.
facts.quote: Each floor formed a single apartment, connected by an elevator and stairs. Horodecki himself occupied the fourth floor of the building, measuring at about 380 m2 (4,100 sq ft).

facts.fact: Its name comes from its decorations of exotic animals and hunting scenes, sculpted by Emilio Sala, because Horodecki was a keen hunter.
facts.quote: The building derives its popular name from the ornate decorations depicting exotic animals and hunting scenes, which were sculpted by Italian architect Emilio Sala, since Horodecki was an avid hunter.

facts.fact: Because it sits on a steep slope, it was built of concrete; it shows three floors at the front and all six at the back.
facts.quote: Due to the steep slope on which the building is situated, it had to be specially designed out of concrete to fit into its foundations correctly. From the front, the building appears to have only three floors. However, from the rear, all of its six floors can be seen.

facts.fact: Sala's sculptures include mermaids, dolphins and frogs on the roof and sinking ships and hunting trophies on the outer walls.
facts.quote: The Italian sculptor Emilio Sala was responsible for both the internal and external sculptural decorations, such as mermaids, dolphins, and frogs on the roof of the building, sinking ships and hunting trophies on the exterior walls, and exuberant interior decorations, such as grand stairways and chandeliers depicting huge catfish strangled in the stems of lotus flowers.

facts.fact: This work earned Horodecki the nickname the Gaudí of Kyiv.
facts.quote: His work on the House with Chimaeras has earned him the nickname of the Gaudí of Kyiv.

facts.fact: Since May 2005 it has been an official presidential residence for ceremonies.
facts.quote: Since May 2005, the building has been an official presidential residence, used for official and diplomatic ceremonies.

facts.fact: The Red Town Hall is Berlin's town hall, near Alexanderplatz, and the seat of the Governing Mayor and the Senate of Berlin.
facts.quote: The Red Town Hall (German: Rotes Rathaus German: [ˈʁoːtəs ˈʁaːtˌhaʊs] ) is the town hall of Berlin, Germany, located in the Mitte district on Rathausstraße near Alexanderplatz. It is the seat to the Governing Mayor of Berlin and the government (the Senate of Berlin) of the state of the city.

facts.fact: Hermann Friedrich Waesemann built it between 1861 and 1869 in the style of the Northern Italian High Renaissance.
facts.quote: The town hall was built between 1861 and 1869 in the style of the Northern Italy High Renaissance by Hermann Friedrich Waesemann.

facts.fact: It was modelled on the Old Town Hall of Toruń, and its tower recalls the cathedral tower at Laon.
facts.quote: It was modelled on the Old Town Hall of Toruń, Poland, while the architecture of the tower is reminiscent of the cathedral tower of the Cathedral of Laon, France.

facts.fact: It replaced several medieval buildings and fills a whole city block.
facts.quote: It replaced several individual buildings dating from the Middle Ages and now occupies an entire city block.

facts.fact: Heavily bombed in the Second World War, it was rebuilt to the original plans between 1951 and 1956.
facts.quote: The building was heavily damaged by Allied bombing in World War II and rebuilt to the original plans between 1951 and 1956.

facts.fact: After German reunification the government of the whole city moved into the building on 1 October 1991.
facts.quote: After German reunification, the administration of reunified Berlin officially moved into the building  on 1 October 1991.

facts.fact: The cathedral is an example of Gothic Revival architecture and is considered a national monument.
facts.quote: An example of Gothic Revival architecture, the cathedral is considered a national monument.

facts.fact: Building began in 1854 with an international competition for a design inspired by the Gothic style of the early 13th century.
facts.quote: Its construction, which spanned nearly a hundred and fifty years, began in 1854 with the laying of a foundation stone and the launch of an international competition for the design of a building inspired by the "Gothic style of the first half of the 13th century".

facts.fact: English entries won the first two prizes, but objections to foreign Anglican architects meant the project went to the Lille architect Charles Leroy.
facts.quote: However, the idea of entrusting the construction of a church in honour of the Virgin to foreign architects of an Anglican confession raised objections. Therefore, the realization of the project fell into the hands of Lille architect Charles Leroy.

facts.fact: Several generations of architects built it in stages from 1856 to 1975.
facts.quote: The cathedral was built in stages under the direction of several generations of architects from 1856 to 1975.

facts.fact: It was completed in 1999 with a modern west front by the architect Pierre-Louis Carlier and the engineer Peter Rice.
facts.quote: It was completed in 1999 by the installation of a modern facade, designed by architect Pierre-Louis Carlier and engineer Peter Rice, with part of the initial programme having been abandoned.

facts.fact: It was built to replace the Collegiate Church of St. Peter, destroyed in the French Revolution, and to give Lille its own bishop.
facts.quote: The first was to rebuild a large church in the heart of the city, after the destruction of the Collegiate Church of St. Peter during the French Revolution, which had housed the statue of Our Lady of the Treille for more than six hundred years. The second was to establish an episcopal see in Lille, which then belonged to the Archdiocese of Cambrai.

facts.fact: The Széchenyi Medicinal Bath in Budapest is one of the largest spa complexes in Europe, fed by two thermal springs.
facts.quote: The Széchenyi Medicinal Bath in Budapest (Hungarian: Széchenyi gyógyfürdő, pronounced [ˈseːt͡ʃeːɲi ˈɟoːɟfyrdøː]) is one of the largest spa complexes in Europe. Its water is supplied by two thermal springs, one at 74 °C (165 °F) and the other at 77 °C (171 °F).

facts.fact: The bath in the City Park was built in the Neo-Baroque style to Győző Czigler's design.
facts.quote: The bath, located in the City Park, was built in Neo-Baroque style to the design of Győző Czigler.

facts.fact: Czigler died in 1905; building began in 1909 under his associates Ede Dvorák and Kálmán Gerster.
facts.quote: Czigler died in 1905, and construction began in 1909 under the direction of his associates Ede Dvorák and Kálmán Gerster.

facts.fact: It opened in June 1913 and was named after István Széchenyi.
facts.quote: During the planning phase from the 1880s, the bath had originally been referred to as the Artesian spa (Artézi fürdő), but when it opened in June 1913 it was named Széchenyi bath (Széchenyi gyógyfürdő) after István Széchenyi.

facts.fact: An extension finished in 1927 added public baths and an outdoor section; the bath now has 3 outdoor and 15 indoor pools.
facts.quote: The extension, completed in 1927, added public baths for men and women and an outdoor section. The bath now has 3 outdoor and 15 indoor pools.

facts.fact: The whole bath was renovated between 1999 and 2009.
facts.quote: Between 1999 and 2009 the Széchenyi thermal bath was refurbished in a complete renovation.

facts.fact: Building work on the Pierre Lassonde Pavilion began in 2013, and it opened to the public in June 2016.
facts.quote: Construction of the Pierre Lassonde Pavilion began in 2013, with the building opened to the public in June 2016.

facts.fact: The pavilion gives a glass-enclosed entrance from Grande Allée to the rest of the museum in Battlefield Park.
facts.quote: The pavilion has a glass-enclosed access point from Grande Allée to the rest of the museum complex further within Battlefield Park.

facts.fact: OMA designed the 14,900 square metre pavilion, led by partners Jason Long and Shohei Shigematsu.
facts.quote: The Office for Metropolitan Architecture designed the 14,900 square metres (160,000 sq ft) pavilion, with the lead partners being Jason Long and Shohei Shigematsu.

facts.fact: It is built mostly of glass and steel, to make the museum open to the public.
facts.quote: The pavilion largely uses glass and steel for its building material, in an effort to foster transparency between the museum and the general public.

facts.fact: It has 2,741 square metres of galleries, a lobby café, a courtyard, a white spiral staircase and a gold-coloured lift.
facts.quote: The pavilion features 2,741 square metres (29,500 sq ft) of gallery space; and also includes a café in its main lobby, a courtyard adjacent to the lobby, a white spiral staircase, and a gold-coloured elevator.

facts.fact: The museum's tunnels were also turned into exhibition spaces during construction.
facts.quote: During the construction of the building, renovations were also undertaken to the museum's tunnel system, transforming them into viewing spaces.

facts.fact: The pavilion holds the museum's contemporary art.
facts.quote: Gérard-Morisset Pavilion houses the museum's historical art collection; the Charles Baillairgé Pavilion houses works of modern art, while the Pierre Lassonde Pavilion houses works of contemporary art.

facts.fact: The pavilion has won many architectural awards.
facts.quote: The Pavilion has revitalized the MNBAQ as it has won numerous architectural awards over the past four years to the end of 2020.

facts.fact: Museum Folkwang is a major collection of 19th- and 20th-century art in Essen, set up in 1922.
facts.quote: Museum Folkwang is a major collection of 19th- and 20th-century art in Essen, Germany. The museum was established in 1922 by merging the Essener Kunstmuseum, which was founded in 1906, and the private Folkwang Museum of the collector and patron Karl Ernst Osthaus in Hagen, founded in 1902.

facts.fact: In 2007 David Chipperfield designed an extension built onto the older building.
facts.quote: In 2007, David Chipperfield designed an extension, which was built onto the older building.

facts.fact: The €55 million rebuilding was paid for by the Alfried Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach Foundation.
facts.quote: A €55m reconstruction was financed by the Alfried Krupp von Bohlen und Halbach Foundation under its chairman Berthold Beitz.

facts.fact: Chipperfield won the City of Essen's international competition in March 2007, against designs by David Adjaye, Volker Staab and Zaha Hadid.
facts.quote: An international architectural competition organized by the City of Essen was won by David Chipperfield (against competing designs by David Adjaye, Volker Staab, and Zaha Hadid) in March 2007.

facts.fact: The new building added 16,000 square metres and opened in January 2010, when Essen and the Ruhr were European Capital of Culture.
facts.quote: The new building, adding 16,000 square metres (170,000 sq ft) to the existing museum, opened in January 2010, when Essen and the Ruhr Area became European Capital of Culture – Ruhr.2010.

facts.fact: The museum also holds the German Poster Museum, with about 340,000 posters.
facts.quote: Museum Folkwang incorporates the Deutsche Plakat Museum (German poster museum), comprising circa 340,000 posters from politics, economy and culture.

facts.fact: The High Museum of Art in Atlanta is the largest museum of visual art in the Southeastern United States.
facts.quote: The High Museum of Art (colloquially the High) is the largest museum for visual art in the Southeastern United States.

facts.fact: Richard Meier's 135,000-square-foot building for the museum opened in 1983.
facts.quote: In 1983, a 135,000-square-foot (12,500 m2) building designed by Richard Meier opened to house the High Museum of Art.

facts.fact: Meier won the 1984 Pritzker Prize after completing the building.
facts.quote: Meier won the 1984 Pritzker Prize after completing the building.

facts.fact: The building has about 52,000 square feet of galleries.
facts.quote: The building contains 135,000 square feet with about 52,000 square feet (4,800 m2) of gallery space.

facts.fact: The High first brought Meier wide recognition, along with his houses and The Atheneum in New Harmony.
facts.quote: Meier first gained recognition for his designs for various houses, for The Atheneum, a visitors center in New Harmony, Indiana (completed 1979), and for the High Museum of Art in Atlanta, Georgia (completed 1983).

facts.fact: In 2005 Renzo Piano added three buildings that more than doubled the museum's size.
facts.quote: In 2005, Renzo Piano designed three new buildings which more than doubled the museum's size to 312,000 square feet (29,000 m2), at a cost of $124 million.

facts.fact: Piano clad his buildings in aluminium panels to match Meier's white enamel facade.
facts.quote: All three new buildings erected as part of the expansion of the High are clad in panels of aluminum to align with Meier's original choice of a white enamel façade.

facts.fact: The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame is a museum and hall of fame in downtown Cleveland, on the shore of Lake Erie.
facts.quote: The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (RRHOF), also simply referred to as the Rock Hall, is a museum and hall of fame located in downtown Cleveland, Ohio, United States, on the shore of Lake Erie.

facts.fact: I. M. Pei designed the museum, which was dedicated on 1 September 1995.
facts.quote: Architect I. M. Pei designed the new museum, and it was dedicated on September 1, 1995.

facts.fact: Pei's idea was a tower with a glass pyramid projecting from it.
facts.quote: Pei came up with the idea of a tower with a glass pyramid protruding from it.

facts.fact: Pei planned the tower at 200 feet but cut it to 162 feet because of the nearby Burke Lakefront Airport.
facts.quote: Pei initially planned the tower to be 200 feet (61 m) high, but was forced to reduce it to 162 feet (49 m) due to the structure's proximity to Burke Lakefront Airport.

facts.fact: The ground was broken on 7 June 1993.
facts.quote: The groundbreaking ceremony for the building took place on June 7, 1993, with Pete Townshend, Chuck Berry, and Billy Joel in attendance.

facts.fact: The inductees are honoured in a wing that juts out over Lake Erie.
facts.quote: Hall of Fame inductees are honored in a special exhibit located in a wing that juts out over Lake Erie.

facts.fact: The building has seven levels.
facts.quote: The building contains seven levels.

facts.fact: In 2020 the museum announced an expansion by a third, led by the firm PAU.
facts.quote: In 2020, the Rock Hall announced plans to renovate and expand its footprint by a third. The architecture firm PAU, founded by Vishaan Chakrabarti, will lead the project.

facts.fact: Yoshio Taniguchi is best known for redesigning the Museum of Modern Art, which reopened on 20 November 2004.
facts.quote: Yoshio Taniguchi (谷口 吉生, Taniguchi Yoshio; 17 October 1937 – 16 December 2024) was a Japanese architect best known for his redesign of the Museum of Modern Art in New York City, which was reopened on 20 November 2004.

facts.fact: In 1997 Taniguchi won the competition against nine other architects, including Rem Koolhaas, Bernard Tschumi and Herzog & de Meuron.
facts.quote: In 1997, Taniguchi won a competition to redesign the Museum of Modern Art, beating out nine other internationally renowned architects, including Rem Koolhaas, Bernard Tschumi, and Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron.

facts.fact: MoMA was Taniguchi's first work outside Japan.
facts.quote: The MoMA commission was Taniguchi's first work outside Japan.

facts.fact: The project nearly doubled MoMA's space for exhibitions and programmes.
facts.quote: The project nearly doubled the space for MoMA's exhibitions and programs, and features 630,000 square feet (59,000 m2) of space.

facts.fact: His plan had two buildings, west and east of an enlarged Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden.
facts.quote: Taniguchi's initial plan called for two structures, one each to the west and east of the Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, which was to be enlarged from its original configuration.

facts.fact: Taniguchi wanted to guide visitors by sight rather than signs, cutting openings in walls to show their thickness and what lies behind.
facts.quote: 'I wanted to direct people visually, not with signs,' said Taniguchi, who cut openings in walls to show their thickness and to expose what lies behind them.

facts.fact: Time's critic called it a subtly updated version of the glass-and-steel box the museum first championed in the 1930s.
facts.quote: "In an era of glamorously expressionist architecture," wrote Time critic Richard Lacayo, MoMA "has opted for a work of what you might call old-fashioned Modernism, clean-lined and rectilinear, a subtly updated version of the glass-and-steel box that the museum first championed in the 1930s, years before that style was adopted for corporate headquarters everywhere."

facts.fact: MoMA reopened on 20 November 2004, and the renovation had a mixed reception.
facts.quote: MoMA reopened on November 20, 2004. The renovation received mixed reception.

facts.fact: The Pergamon Museum is a listed building on Museum Island in Berlin, built from 1910 to 1930 to plans by Alfred Messel and Ludwig Hoffmann in a Stripped Classicism style.
facts.quote: The Pergamon Museum (German: Pergamonmuseum; pronounced [ˈpɛʁ.ɡa.mɔn.muˌzeː.ʊm] ) is a listed building on the Museum Island in the historic centre of Berlin, Germany. It was built from 1910 to 1930 by order of Emperor Wilhelm II and according to plans by Alfred Messel and Ludwig Hoffmann in Stripped Classicism style.

facts.fact: With the rest of Museum Island it joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1999.
facts.quote: As part of the Museum Island complex, the Pergamon Museum was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1999 because of its architecture and testimony to the evolution of museums as architectural and social phenomena.

facts.fact: Messel began designing the large three-wing building in 1906; after his death in 1909 Ludwig Hoffmann took over and it opened in 1930.
facts.quote: Alfred Messel began a design for the large three-wing building in 1906. After his death in 1909 his friend Ludwig Hoffman took charge of the project and construction began in 1910, continuing during the First World War (1918) and the great inflation of the 1920s. The completed building was opened in 1930.

facts.fact: Hoffmann raised the eaves, flattened the pediment and added a metope and triglyph frieze.
facts.quote: The changes made by Hoffmann on the building's exterior had a restraining and moderating effect. The most noticeable were the raising of the eaves, the flattening of the pediment and the addition of a metope and triglyph frieze.

facts.fact: It was built to show ancient architecture, German art after antiquity, and Middle Eastern and Islamic art.
facts.quote: Wilhelm von Bode, director of the Kaiser-Friedrich-Museum, initiated plans to build a new museum nearby to accommodate ancient architecture, German post-antiquity art, and Middle Eastern and Islamic art.

facts.fact: Its displays include the Pergamon Altar, with a 113-metre frieze, and the Gate of Miletus.
facts.quote: The main exhibits are the Pergamon Altar from the 2nd century BC, with a 113-metre (371 ft) long sculptural frieze depicting the struggle of the gods and the giants, and the Gate of Miletus from Roman antiquity.

facts.fact: Oswald Mathias Ungers won a 2000 competition to redevelop the museum; his plan controversially proposes large changes to buildings unchanged since 1930.
facts.quote: An architectural competition in 2000 was won by Oswald Mathias Ungers from Cologne. The Pergamon Museum will be redeveloped according to his plan, which controversially proposes large alterations to buildings unchanged since 1930.

facts.fact: The museum closed fully in October 2023 for renovation expected to take 14 to 20 years.
facts.quote: In October 2023, the museum was completely closed for visitors, and is expected to remain mostly closed for 14 to 20 years – until 2037 to 2043 – for the execution of comprehensive renovation works.

facts.fact: The Museum of Pop Culture in Seattle was founded by Paul Allen in 2000 as the Experience Music Project.
facts.quote: It was founded by Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen in 2000 as the Experience Music Project.

facts.fact: It stands on the Seattle Center campus next to the Space Needle, and the Seattle Center Monorail runs through the building.
facts.quote: MOPOP is located on the campus of Seattle Center, adjacent to the Space Needle and the Seattle Center Monorail, which runs through the building.

facts.fact: Frank Gehry designed it in sheet metal, like his Guggenheim Bilbao and Walt Disney Concert Hall.
facts.quote: The structure itself was designed by Frank Gehry and resembles many of his firm's other works in its sheet-metal construction, such as Guggenheim Museum Bilbao, Walt Disney Concert Hall, and Gehry Tower.

facts.fact: Much of the building material is left exposed inside, and the building has 140,000 square feet on a 35,000-square-foot footprint.
facts.quote: Much of the building material is exposed in the building's interior. The building contains 140,000 square feet (13,000 m2), with a 35,000-square-foot (3,300 m2) footprint.

facts.fact: Gehry worked from the shapes of electric guitars: his team collected pictures of Stratocasters and guitar bodies.
facts.quote: Gehry himself had in fact made the comparison: "We started collecting pictures of Stratocasters, bringing in guitar bodies, drawing on those shapes in developing our ideas."

facts.fact: The name of the central Sky Church pays homage to Jimi Hendrix.
facts.quote: The name of the museum's central Sky Church pays homage to Jimi Hendrix.

facts.fact: Seattle greeted it with a mix of acclaim for Gehry and derision for this building.
facts.quote: The architecture was greeted by Seattle residents with a mixture of acclaim for Gehry and derision for this particular edifice.

facts.fact: The outside mixes textures and colours including gold, silver, deep red, blue and purple.
facts.quote: The building's exterior, which features a fusion of textures and colors including gold, silver, deep red, blue and a "shimmering purple haze", has been declared "an apt representation of the American rock experience."

facts.fact: In 2005 the museum board chose David Chipperfield to design the expansion, with Michel Desvigne as landscape architect and HOK as architect of record.
facts.quote: Plans to expand the museum, which existed in the 1995 Forest Park Master Plan and the museum's 2000 Strategic Plan, began in earnest in 2005, when the museum board selected the British architect Sir David Chipperfield to design the expansion; Michel Desvigne was selected as landscape architect. The St. Louis-based firm, Hellmuth, Obata, and Kassabaum (HOK) was the architect of record to work with the construction team.

facts.fact: The new wing is attached to Cass Gilbert's beaux-arts gallery of 1904.
facts.quote: The Saint Louis Art Museum project in Saint Louis, Missouri, United States (2005–2013) involved building a major new wing attached to a landmark of American architecture, the gallery built by beaux-arts architect Cass Gilbert in 1904.

facts.fact: Its ground level matches the main floor of the Gilbert Building.
facts.quote: The new building by Chipperfield, with 9,000 square metres of space, harmonizes smoothly with the classic building; its ground level is the same as that of the main floor of the Gilbert Building.

facts.fact: A roof of concrete coffers controls the light entering the galleries.
facts.quote: The walls are dark concrete were poured and polished in place, and the roof of concrete caissons is designed to modify the light entering the galleries.

facts.fact: The dark grey polished concrete walls are speckled with the same kind of sandstone used in the Gilbert building.
facts.quote: To give the facade a distinctive look which also blended with the Gilbert building, Chipperfield speckled the dark grey polished concrete walls with fragments of the same kind of sandstone used in the Gilbert building.

facts.fact: The expanded museum opened in summer 2013.
facts.quote: The expanded facility opened in the summer of 2013.

facts.fact: Andy Goldsworthy's Stone Sea, 25 limestone arches, fills a sunken courtyard between the old and new buildings.
facts.quote: In the context of the museum's 2013 expansion, British artist Andy Goldsworthy created Stone Sea, a site-specific work for a narrow space between the old and new buildings. Twenty-five tightly packed, ten-foot-high arches made of native limestone rise in a sunken courtyard.

facts.fact: Kenzo Tange designed the former Kurashiki City Hall in 1960.
facts.quote: Kenzo Tange, winner of the 1987 Pritzker Prize for architecture, designed the former Kurashiki City Hall in 1960.

facts.fact: Hearst Castle is a historic estate in San Simeon, California, conceived by William Randolph Hearst and his architect Julia Morgan and built between 1919 and 1947.
facts.quote: Hearst Castle, known formally as La Cuesta Encantada (Spanish for 'The Enchanted Hill'), is a historic estate in San Simeon, located on the Central Coast of California. Conceived by William Randolph Hearst, the publishing tycoon, and his architect Julia Morgan, the castle was built between 1919 and 1947.

facts.fact: Morgan worked closely with Hearst for over twenty years, and building went on almost without pause from 1920 to 1939.
facts.quote: She worked in close collaboration with Hearst for over twenty years; the castle was under almost continual construction from 1920 until 1939, with work resuming after the end of World War II until Hearst's final departure in 1947.

facts.fact: Hearst bought architectural pieces from Western Europe, especially Spain, including ceilings, fireplaces and whole monasteries, and much was built into the castle.
facts.quote: Foremost among his purchases were architectural elements from Western Europe, particularly Spain; over thirty ceilings, doorcases, fireplaces and mantels, entire monasteries, paneling and a medieval tithe barn were purchased, shipped to Hearst's Brooklyn warehouses and transported on to California. Much was then incorporated into the fabric of Hearst Castle.

facts.fact: Hearst asked Morgan to model the Casa Grande towers on a church in Ronda, Spain.
facts.quote: He particularly admired a church in Ronda, Spain and asked Morgan to model the Casa Grande towers after it.

facts.fact: Its style blends Southern Spanish Renaissance, Revival and Mediterranean examples.
facts.quote: This blend of Southern Spanish Renaissance, Revival and Mediterranean examples became San Simeon's defining style; "something a little different than other people are doing out in California".

facts.fact: The estate has 42 bedrooms, 61 bathrooms, 127 acres of gardens, indoor and outdoor pools, a cinema and an airfield.
facts.quote: Hearst Castle has a total of 42 bedrooms, 61 bathrooms, 19 sitting rooms, 127 acres (0.5 km2) of gardens, indoor and outdoor swimming pools, tennis courts, a movie theater, an airfield and, during Hearst's lifetime, the world's largest private zoo.

facts.fact: Because Hearst kept changing the design and money ran short in the 1930s, the complex was never finished.
facts.quote: As a consequence of Hearst's persistent design changes, and financial difficulties in the early and later 1930s, the complex was never finished.

facts.fact: Concrete was the main structural material of the houses and their outbuildings.
facts.quote: Water was also essential for the production of concrete, the main structural component of the houses and their ancillary buildings.

facts.fact: It is now a California State Park and a National Historic Landmark.
facts.quote: Today, Hearst Castle is a museum open to the public as a California State Park and registered as a National Historic Landmark and California Historical Landmark.

facts.fact: The Mikhailovsky Palace is a grand ducal palace on Arts Square in Saint Petersburg, in the Empire style of neoclassicism.
facts.quote: The Mikhailovsky Palace (Russian: Михайловский дворец, romanized: Mikhailovskiy dvorets) is a grand ducal palace in Saint Petersburg, Russia. It is located on Arts Square and is an example of Empire style neoclassicism.

facts.fact: It now houses the main building of the Russian Museum.
facts.quote: The palace currently houses the main building of the Russian Museum and displays its collections of early, folk, eighteenth, and nineteenth century art.

facts.fact: Carlo Rossi drew up the designs in 1817.
facts.quote: The designs were drawn up by Carlo Rossi in 1817.

facts.fact: Rossi planned a whole new ensemble: the palace, a square and two new streets.
facts.quote: Rossi set out to develop a new architectural ensemble, which would include not only a new palace, but a square and two new streets, Inzhenernaya and Mikhailovskaya.

facts.fact: Building took six years and cost 7,875,000 rubles, more than half of it spent on decoration.
facts.quote: Its construction had taken six years, at the expense of 7,875,000 rubles.  Of this sum approximately 4 million rubles, more than half the total cost, was spent on its decoration.

facts.fact: The palace is a central block with two service wings.
facts.quote: The palace consists of a central block with two wings, housing the service spaces.

facts.fact: The facade has a rusticated ground floor and a loggia with eight Corinthian columns carrying a triangular pediment.
facts.quote: Its facade consists of a rusticated lower floor below the piano nobile portico, a loggia with a three-quarter eight-columned Corinthian colonnade supporting a triangular pediment with armour decorations by Stepan Pimenov and Vasily Demut-Malinovsky.

facts.fact: A new extension, the Benois wing, was added in the 1910s.
facts.quote: One wing was demolished and rebuilt, later becoming the Russian Museum of Ethnography, while a new extension, the Benois wing, was added in the 1910s.

facts.fact: The State Historical Museum is a museum of Russian history between Red Square and Manege Square in Moscow.
facts.quote: The State Historical Museum (Russian: Государственный исторический музей, ГИМ, romanized: Gosudarstvennyy istoricheskiy muzey, GIM) of Russia is a museum of Russian history located between Red Square and Manege Square in Moscow.

facts.fact: Its site was once occupied by the Principal Medicine Store, built for Peter the Great in the Moscow Baroque style.
facts.quote: The place where the museum now stands was formerly occupied by the Principal Medicine Store, built by order of Peter the Great in the Moscow Baroque style.

facts.fact: After a long competition, the design went to Vladimir Sherwood.
facts.quote: After a prolonged competition, the project was handed over to Vladimir Osipovich Shervud (or Sherwood, 1833–97).

facts.fact: The building was built to Sherwood's neo-Russian design between 1875 and 1881, and the first 11 halls opened in 1883.
facts.quote: The present structure was built based on Sherwood's neo-Russian design between 1875 and 1881. The first 11 exhibit halls officially opened in 1883 during a visit from the tsar and his wife.

facts.fact: Its interiors were richly decorated in the Russian Revival style by artists including Viktor Vasnetsov and Ivan Aivazovsky; in Soviet times the murals were plastered over.
facts.quote: Its interiors were intricately decorated in the Russian Revival style by such artists as Viktor Vasnetsov, Henryk Siemiradzki, and Ivan Aivazovsky. During the Soviet period, the murals were proclaimed gaudy and were plastered over.

facts.fact: Sherwood was one of the most visible architects of the Russian Revival under Alexander III.
facts.quote: Vladimir Osipovich became one of the most visible architects of the Alexander III version of Russian Revival, also noted for his Plevna Chapel and Nikolay Pirogov memorial in Moscow.

facts.fact: Since spring 2007 all 40 halls have been open to the public.
facts.quote: Since spring 2007, for the first time in the history of The State Historical Museum, all 40 halls have been open to the public.

facts.fact: Vienna City Hall is a Gothic Revival building by Friedrich von Schmidt, built between 1872 and 1883 on the Rathausplatz off the Ringstrasse.
facts.quote: The Vienna City Hall (German: Wiener Rathaus; [ʁaːtˌhaʊs]) is the town hall of Vienna, Austria, located in the Innere Stadt on the Rathausplatz, off the Ringstrasse. The Gothic Revival building was designed by Friedrich von Schmidt and constructed between 1872 and 1883.

facts.fact: It houses the offices of the Mayor of Vienna and the city and state government.
facts.quote: It houses the offices of the Mayor of Vienna, as well as the city and state government.

facts.fact: A competition for a new city hall was held in 1868, after the city walls were demolished to build the Ringstrasse.
facts.quote: With the demolition of city walls between 1858 and 1865 to build the Ringstraße, a competition for a new city hall was held in 1868.

facts.fact: It is 152 metres long and 127 metres wide, with 1,575 rooms and 2,035 windows.
facts.quote: It is 152 meters long and 127 meters wide, containing 1,575 rooms and 2,035 windows.

facts.fact: It is a freestanding Neo-Gothic building with Renaissance elements, facing the Rathauspark.
facts.quote: The Rathaus is a freestanding Neo-Gothic building with Renaissance elements, located on Rathausplatz with the Rathauspark in front, consisting of two parks on either side of the square.

facts.fact: The main facade has a central tower with four smaller side towers and open arcades on the ground floor.
facts.quote: The main facade features a central Risalit with a large tower and four smaller side towers, complemented by open arcades on the ground floor.

facts.fact: The 98-metre tower is crowned by the Rathausmann, a symbol of Vienna.
facts.quote: The 98-meter high tower is crowned by the Rathausmann, a symbolic figure of Vienna.

facts.fact: The Festsaal is Austria's largest historic hall, given a Renaissance-style barrel vault so it would not look like a church.
facts.quote: Above the Volkshalle, the Festsaal is Austria’s largest historic hall, designed with a Renaissance-style barrel vault to avoid a church-like appearance.

facts.fact: The building has seven courtyards, the central Arcaded Courtyard being the most prominent.
facts.quote: The Rathaus features seven courtyards, with the central Arcaded Courtyard being the most prominent.

facts.fact: The Marin County Civic Center is a government complex in San Rafael, California, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright and Taliesin Associated Architects.
facts.quote: The Marin County Civic Center is a governmental complex in San Rafael, the county seat of Marin County, California, United States. Designed by Frank Lloyd Wright and Taliesin Associated Architects (TAA), the 140-acre (57 ha) complex consists of several buildings constructed between 1960 and 1976.

facts.fact: Wright died with the plans 90% complete, and Taliesin Associated Architects finished the design.
facts.quote: Wright died the next month, at which point the plans were 90% complete. Taliesin Associated Architects (TAA), the successor firm to Wright's practice, was enlisted to complete the Civic Center, and Green and Wright's son-in-law William Wesley Peters of TAA took over the design.

facts.fact: Wright chose to build the main building on the hills rather than the flat land.
facts.quote: When the complex was being designed, its architect Frank Lloyd Wright decided to erect the main building on the hills.

facts.fact: The Administration Building sits on three hills, so a road runs underneath it.
facts.quote: The Administration Building is constructed on three hills. As a result, an access road to the complex's parking area (now Peter Behr Drive) runs underneath the Administration Building.

facts.fact: The main building has pink stucco walls with tiers of arches under a blue roof.
facts.quote: The main building has pink stucco walls with several levels of arches, topped by a blue roof.

facts.fact: Its two wings, the Administration Building and the Hall of Justice, meet at a 120° angle at a rotunda with a spire.
facts.quote: The shorter Administration Building wing and the longer Hall of Justice are joined at a 120° angle by a rotunda with a spire.

facts.fact: Inside are county offices, courtrooms, atria in both wings, and a library and cafeteria in the rotunda.
facts.quote: Inside are county offices, courtrooms in the Hall of Justice, atria in both wings, and a library and cafeteria in the rotunda.

facts.fact: The main building, lagoon and post office are a National Historic Landmark.
facts.quote: The Civic Center's main building, lagoon, and post office are designated as a California Historical Landmark and National Historic Landmark.

facts.fact: St. Peter's at Klippan (1963–66) was one of two churches Lewerentz designed in the last decade of his life, which revived his career.
facts.quote: In the last decade of his life he designed two churches, St. Mark's at Björkhagen in Stockholm (1956) and St. Peter's at Klippan in Scania (1963–66), which revived his career in architecture.

facts.fact: The church sits in a suburban setting on the edge of the small town of Klippan in southern Sweden.
facts.quote: St. Peter's at Klippan sits in a suburban setting on the periphery of this small town in southern Sweden.

facts.fact: The altar stands opposite the west doors.
facts.quote: The orientation of the church is correct, with the altar standing opposite the west doors.

facts.fact: The church is square, suggesting a more intimate ritual of people standing in a circle, going back to early Christianity.
facts.quote: It is square in shape, suggesting a more intimate ritual in the tradition of circonstantes (standing in a circle), which harkens back to early Christianity.

facts.fact: The church was completed in 1966.
facts.quote: The Church of St. Peter, designed by Sigurd Lewerentz, was completed in 1966.

facts.fact: The East Building was built in the 1970s, funded by Paul Mellon and Ailsa Mellon Bruce.
facts.quote: The Gallery's East Building was constructed in the 1970s on much of the remaining land left over from the original congressional action. Andrew Mellon's children, Paul Mellon and Ailsa Mellon Bruce, funded the building.

facts.fact: Designed by I. M. Pei, it was completed in 1978 and opened on 1 June that year by President Jimmy Carter.
facts.quote: Designed by architect I. M. Pei, the contemporary structure was completed in 1978 and was opened on June 1 of that year by President Jimmy Carter.

facts.fact: The design won a National Honor Award from the American Institute of Architects in 1981.
facts.quote: The design received a National Honor Award from the American Institute of Architects in 1981.

facts.fact: Pei split the trapezoidal site into two triangles, one for public galleries and one for a library, offices and a study centre.
facts.quote: In contrast, the design of the East Building, by architect I. M. Pei, is geometrical, dividing the trapezoidal shape of the site into two triangles: one contains public galleries, and the other houses a library, offices, and a study center.

facts.fact: The triangle is repeated throughout the building, in every dimension.
facts.quote: The triangles establish a motif that is echoed throughout the building, realized in every dimension.

facts.fact: Its central feature is a high atrium of 16,000 square feet.
facts.quote: The East Building's central feature is a high atrium designed as an open interior court that is enclosed by a sculptural space spanning 16,000 sq ft (1,500 m2).

facts.fact: It is built of the same Tennessee marble as the West Building and lines up with that building's main axis.
facts.quote: The atrium is centered on the same axis that forms the circulation spine for the West Building and is constructed in the same Tennessee marble.

facts.fact: It is clad in 3-inch-thick pink marble panels, and an $85 million restoration of the facade began in 2011.
facts.quote: Beginning in 2011, NGA undertook an $85 million restoration of the East Building's façade. The East Building is clad in 3-inch (7.6 cm) thick pink marble panels.

facts.fact: Kresge Auditorium at MIT was designed by Eero Saarinen, begun in 1953 and dedicated in 1955.
facts.quote: It was designed by the Finnish-American architect Eero Saarinen, with ground-breaking in 1953 and dedication in 1955.

facts.fact: Saarinen designed it together with the nearby MIT Chapel, the two separated by a lawn called the Kresge Oval.
facts.quote: Saarinen designed Kresge Auditorium in tandem with his nearby MIT Chapel; the two buildings are separated by a green space called the Kresge Oval.

facts.fact: The roof is a thin shell of reinforced concrete, one-eighth of a sphere, 50 feet high, cut by glass walls so it touches the ground at only three points.
facts.quote: The auditorium is defined by an elegant thin-shell structure of reinforced concrete, one-eighth of a sphere rising to a height of 50 feet (15 m), and sliced away by sheer glass curtain walls so that it comes to earth on only three points.

facts.fact: Thin-shell concrete was new at the time; the dome is proportionally thinner than an eggshell.
facts.quote: Thin-shelled concrete technology was innovative for the times; the dome is proportionately thinner than an eggshell.

facts.fact: Copper later replaced the lead roofing, and the walls now carry part of the roof load.
facts.quote: Copper replaced the lead at that time, and the walls now carry part of the roof load.

facts.fact: On a round red brick platform, the dome holds a 1,226-seat concert hall and a 177-seat theatre below.
facts.quote: Sitting on a circular red brick platform, the dome contains a concert hall (with seating for 1,226 people), plus a lower level that houses a small theater (seating 177), two rehearsal rooms, dressing rooms, offices, bathrooms, and lounges.

facts.fact: With no columns under the dome, every seat has a clear view.
facts.quote: Every seat in the concert hall has an unobstructed view, since there are no interior supports for the overarching dome.

facts.fact: Instead of a plaster ceiling, hanging acoustic "clouds" absorb and direct sound.
facts.quote: Working with acoustical architects Bolt, Beranek and Newman, architect Saarinen employed free-hanging acoustic "clouds" that absorb and direct sound, instead of a traditional plaster ceiling.

facts.fact: Josef Hoffmann built the Sanatorium Purkersdorf in 1904–05 for the industrialist Victor Zuckerkandl, in the style of the Vienna Secession.
facts.quote: It was built in 1904-05 by the architect Josef Hoffmann for the industrialist Victor Zuckerkandl and is an example of the style of the Viennese Secession in architecture.

facts.fact: The original furnishings were made by the Wiener Werkstätte, with which Hoffmann was involved.
facts.quote: The original furnishings were made by the Wiener Werkstätte with which the architect Hoffmann was involved.

facts.fact: It was more a hotel than a hospital, and became a social and artistic meeting place for Viennese society.
facts.quote: The sanitorium was more of a hotel than hospital and turned into a social and artistic venue of Viennese society.

facts.fact: Silence, light, air and a rational building with almost no ornament were meant to cure nervous illnesses.
facts.quote: Through silence, light and air, and the rationality of the facility with ornament reduced to a minimum, cures of the new illnesses such as nervousness, and hysteria were sought.

facts.fact: In 1926 Leopold Bauer added a floor, against Hoffmann's wishes.
facts.quote: In 1926, against the will of Josef Hoffmann, the architect Leopold Bauer heightened the building with another floor, which impaired the original artistic conception.

facts.fact: A 1995 renovation removed that added floor and restored the original look.
facts.quote: In 1995, an external renovation took place, whereby the upper floor added by Leopold Bauer was removed and the original appearance was restored.

facts.fact: Hoffmann's first great work, it moved away from Arts and Crafts and was a major precedent for modern architecture.
facts.quote: In 1905, Hoffmann finished his first great work in the town of Purkersdorf near Vienna, the Sanatorium Purkersdorf. It was a distinct move away from the Arts and Crafts style, as a major precedent and inspiration for the modern architecture that would develop in the first half of the 20th century, It had the clarity, simplicity, and logic that foreshadowed Neue Sachlichkeit.

facts.fact: The MIT Chapel is a non-denominational chapel by Eero Saarinen, dedicated in 1955 and completed in 1956.
facts.quote: The MIT Chapel (dedicated 1955, completed in 1956) is a non-denominational chapel designed by noted architect Eero Saarinen.

facts.fact: From outside it is a plain, windowless brick cylinder in a shallow concrete moat.
facts.quote: From the outside, the chapel is a simple, windowless brick cylinder set inside a very shallow concrete moat.

facts.fact: It is 50 feet across and 30 feet high, topped by an aluminium spire.
facts.quote: It is 50 feet (15 m) in diameter and 30 feet (9.1 m) high, and topped by an aluminum spire.

facts.fact: Saarinen chose rough, imperfect bricks for texture.
facts.quote: Saarinen chose bricks that were rough and imperfect to create a textured effect.

facts.fact: Inside, the windowless walls are undulating brick.
facts.quote: Windowless interior walls are undulating brick.

facts.fact: A full-height metal sculpture by Harry Bertoia falls from a round skylight to a plain marble altar.
facts.quote: Like a cascade of light, a full-height metal sculpture by Harry Bertoia glitters from the circular skylight down to a small, unadorned marble altar.

facts.fact: Daylight enters through low slits in the walls, catching light reflected from the moat.
facts.quote: Natural light filters upward from shallow slits in the walls catching rippling reflected light from the moat; this dim ambient light is complemented by artificial lighting.

facts.fact: The spire and bell tower were designed by the sculptor Theodore Roszak and added in 1956.
facts.quote: The chapel's curving spire and bell tower were designed by the sculptor Theodore Roszak and added in 1956.

facts.fact: The Berlin store was designed by Jean Nouvel, built between 1991 and 1995, and opened in February 1996.
facts.quote: Berlin, Germany – Opened in February 1996, the store was designed by Jean Nouvel with construction taking place between 1991 and 1995.

facts.fact: It stood on Friedrichstraße, two blocks south of the Unter den Linden U-Bahn station.
facts.quote: The store was located on Friedrichstraße two blocks south of the Under den Linden U-Bahn station.

facts.fact: The store closed in July 2024.
facts.quote: The store was closed in July 2024.

facts.fact: Geisel Library is the main library of the University of California, San Diego.
facts.quote: Geisel Library is the main library building of the University of California, San Diego.

facts.fact: William Pereira designed it, and it opened in 1970 as the Central Library.
facts.quote: The library was designed by William Pereira and opened in 1970 as the Central Library.

facts.fact: It was designed to sit at the head of a canyon; its arches and floors are meant to look like hands holding up a stack of books.
facts.quote: The distinctive original building was designed in the late 1960s by William Pereira to sit at the head of a canyon. The building's arches, in combination with the design of the individual floors, are intended to look like hands holding up a stack of books.

facts.fact: The building centres on a rounded tower, so the most shelving could be reached quickly from the middle.
facts.quote: The proposed building was designed around a spheroidal tower, to maximize the stacks area that could be accessed in a given time from the center.

facts.fact: Pereira first planned a steel frame, but cost made him switch to reinforced concrete, which allowed a more sculptural form.
facts.quote: Pereira originally conceived of a mushroom-shaped, steel-framed building, but the projected construction and maintenance costs forced him to switch to a reinforced concrete structure. This change of material presented an opportunity for a more sculptural design, as well as opening up interior spaces that would have been bisected by steel trusses.

facts.fact: The tower rises 8 storeys to 110 feet.
facts.quote: Its tower rises 8 stories to a height of 110 ft (33.5 m).

facts.fact: Its architecture has been described as sitting between brutalism and futurism.
facts.quote: The building has been described by Architecture Daily as occupying "a fascinating nexus between brutalism and futurism".

facts.fact: An underground addition by Gunnar Birkerts, funded in 1990, was deliberately kept subordinate to the original building.
facts.quote: The expansion project was ultimately funded in 1990, at which point the original plan had been discarded in favor of a subterranean addition onto the front of the library, designed by architect Gunnar Birkerts. In keeping with the original master plan, the addition was "deliberately designed to be subordinated to the strong, geometrical form of the existing library".

facts.fact: The Maison du Peuple in Clichy was built from 1935 to 1939 by the architects Eugène Beaudouin and Marcel Lods, the engineer Vladimir Bodiansky and Jean Prouvé.
facts.quote: The Maison du Peuple (French pronunciation: [mɛzɔ̃ dy pœpl], lit. 'House of the People') in Clichy, classified as official historical monument of France (Monument Historique) since 1983, is a building built from 1935 to 1939 in the Parisian suburb of Clichy-la-Garenne by the architects Eugène Beaudouin, Marcel Lods, the engineer Vladimir Bodiansky and Jean Prouvé.

facts.fact: In 1935 the mayor of Clichy held a competition to roof over the outdoor market on Rue de Lorraine.
facts.quote: In 1935, the mayor of Clichy, Charles Auffray, launched a competition for architects to cover the outdoor market in Rue de Lorraine.

facts.fact: The design kept the market on the ground floor and added a floor above for offices and a 1,000-seat multipurpose hall.
facts.quote: The architects Beaudouin and Lods, associated with the engineer Vladimir Bodianski, proposed an innovative project: they intended to put the space to maximum use and therefore planned to leave the market on the ground floor while adding a floor on top of it that could house offices and a multipurpose room with 1,000 seats.

facts.fact: The hall could become a cinema, with movable partitions, a retractable floor and a retractable roof.
facts.quote: The room was meant to be multi-functional: it could be transformed into a cinema, in a fully modular build with partitions, a retractable floor and a retractable roof, in a marvel of ingenuity.

facts.fact: Prouvé's curtain walls were used here for the first time: the walls carry no load and simply hang from the structure.
facts.quote: Prouvé provided original technical solutions, the most exemplary of which remains the curtain walls, used for the first time in Clichy: the walls are not load-bearing, but instead simply suspended from the structure.

facts.fact: The building was restored from 1993 under Hervé Baptiste.
facts.quote: The restoration of the building was undertaken in 1993 under the leadership of Hervé Baptiste.

facts.fact: MVRDV designed the Dutch Pavilion for Expo 2000 in Hanover between 1997 and 2000, one of the firm's early built works.
facts.quote: Other early built works include the Wozoco housing in Amsterdam (1994–1997) and the Dutch Pavilion at the Hannover World Exhibition Expo 2000 (1997–2000).

facts.fact: At 36 metres it was the Expo's tallest structure, on the theme "Holland creates Space".
facts.quote: The theme of the 36 m high building (the Expo's tallest structure) was "Holland creates Space".

facts.fact: Six Dutch landscapes were stacked on top of each other to show how a small country can make the most of little space.
facts.quote: Six Holland eco-system landscapes were stacked to showcase how a country can make the most out of a small space.

facts.fact: Visitors entered at ground level and moved up by large outdoor staircases wrapped around the building.
facts.quote: Guests entered on the ground floor and moved through the exhibit space via grand exterior staircases that wrapped around the building.

facts.fact: The top level held a small lake ringed by wind turbines that powered the building.
facts.quote: The top level contained a small lake surrounded with windmills that generated power for the building.

facts.fact: It was one of the most popular pavilions and won international acclaim.
facts.quote: Netherlands was located at '3' Europa Boulevard, and the Dutch pavilion was one of the most popular buildings, winning international acclaim, and was designed by the firm MVRDV.

facts.fact: The building sat empty and was partly looted until 2020, when MVRDV announced plans to turn it into offices and student housing.
facts.quote: The building sat empty and was partially looted with windows smashed and garbage everywhere, until 2020, when MVRDV announced the plan to transform the building into an office and student housing complex.

facts.fact: Kenzō Tange's Kagawa Prefectural Government Hall on Shikoku was completed in 1958.
facts.quote: The Kagawa Prefectural Government Hall on the island of Shikoku was completed in 1958.

facts.fact: Its expressive construction has been compared to the Daibutsu style of Tōdai-ji in Nara.
facts.quote: Its expressive construction could be likened to the Daibutsu style seen at the Tōdai-ji in Nara.

facts.fact: The columns on the facade carry only vertical loads, so Tange could make them thin and leave more of the surface for glass.
facts.quote: The columns on the elevation bore only vertical loads so Tange was able to design them to be thin, maximising the surfaces for glazing.

facts.fact: It has been called one of his finest projects, though at the time it was criticised for leaning too heavily on tradition.
facts.quote: Although the hall has been called one of his finest projects, it drew criticism at the time of its construction for relying too heavily on tradition.

facts.fact: The Marugame Genichiro-Inokuma Museum of Contemporary Art opened in Marugame, Kagawa Prefecture, in 1991, in a building designed by Yoshio Taniguchi.
facts.quote: Marugame Genichiro-Inokuma Museum of Contemporary Art (丸亀市猪熊弦一郎現代美術館, Marugame-shi Inokuma Genichirō Gendai Bijutsukan) (MIMOCA) opened in Marugame, Kagawa Prefecture, Japan, in 1991. Architect Yoshio Taniguchi designed the museum building.

facts.fact: Its collection is some twenty thousand works given by the artist Gen'ichirō Inokuma, alongside exhibitions of other contemporary artists.
facts.quote: The museum collection comprises some twenty thousand works donated by artist Gen’ichirō Inokuma. Special exhibitions of works by other contemporary artists are also staged.

facts.fact: Taniguchi's father, Yoshirō Taniguchi, and Inokuma had worked closely together.
facts.quote: In 1991, the Marugame Genichiro-Inokuma Museum of Contemporary Art (MIMOCA), designed by Yoshio Taniguchi (his father, Yoshirō Taniguchi, and Inokuma were close collaborators), was opened.

facts.fact: With Benesse Art Site Naoshima and the Nagi Museum, it has become an important centre for contemporary art in the Chūgoku and Shikoku regions.
facts.quote: Today, along with Benesse Art Site Naoshima (which includes the Benesse House Museum, opened in 1992), and the Nagi Museum of Contemporary Art (opened in 1994), the Marugame Genichiro-Inokuma Museum of Contemporary Art has become an important transmitter of contemporary art in the Chūgoku and Shikoku regions.

facts.fact: Keeling House is a 16-storey block of flats in Bethnal Green, London, by Denys Lasdun, completed in 1957 as four blocks of maisonettes around a central service tower.
facts.quote: Keeling House is a 16-storey block of flats located on Claredale Street in Bethnal Green, London, England. It was designed by Denys Lasdun and completed in 1957 as a cluster of four blocks of maisonettes arranged around a central service tower.

facts.fact: Lasdun wanted to give residents the sense of place and good neighbourliness he saw in traditional Victorian terraced streets.
facts.quote: Lasdun was concerned that earlier modernist designs did not take sufficient account of what made neighbourhoods work. He sought to give residents a sense of place and belonging, replicating the good relations between neighbours which he noticed in traditional Victorian terraced streets.

facts.fact: Each home was a maisonette, similar inside to an East End house.
facts.quote: Each dwelling was a maisonette rather than a flat, similar inside to an East End house.

facts.fact: Its four wings look onto each other to encourage contact between neighbours.
facts.quote: Unlike a flat slab or tower block, he designed Keeling House with four wings that each look onto another, encouraging contact between neighbours.

facts.fact: Between the lift tower and the front doors, tenants passed shared drying areas meant for meeting; but balconies face outward for privacy.
facts.quote: Between the central lift tower and the front doors of the apartments, tenants had to pass communal 'drying areas' for laundry and storage, where he hoped that social interchange would be as natural as in the streets below. However, he also designed the homes for privacy; the balconies face outward and do not look onto one another.

facts.fact: It was listed Grade II* in 1993, the second post-war council housing to be listed.
facts.quote: In 1993, the building was designated a Grade II* listed building. This was the second example of post-war council housing being granted a listing, closely after Neave Brown's Alexandra road estate.

facts.fact: It was converted into private flats between 1999 and 2001, with a glass foyer and eight penthouses on the old service roof.
facts.quote: It was converted into luxury apartments between 1999 and 2001. Key features of the renovation include a striking glass foyer with external water feature designed by local architects Munkenbeck and Marshall, and eight penthouses on what had previously been the service roof of a 15-storey building.

facts.fact: The redevelopment won an RIBA Award in 2002.
facts.quote: The redevelopment won an RIBA Award in 2002 and a Civic Trust commendation.

facts.fact: Immeuble Molitor is an apartment building by Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret, built between 1931 and 1934.
facts.quote: Immeuble Molitor is an apartment building designed by Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret and built between 1931 and 1934.

facts.fact: Le Corbusier lived in the building from its completion until his death in 1965.
facts.quote: Le Corbusier lived in the building from its completion until his death in 1965.

facts.fact: The eight-storey building has fifteen apartments and uses four of Le Corbusier's five points: free plan, columns instead of load-bearing walls, free facade and roof garden.
facts.quote: Between July and October 1931, Le Corbusier and Jeanneret designed an eight-story building with fifteen apartments, with two or three units per level. The design applied four of Le Corbusier's five points of modern architecture – free floor plan, structure supported by columns rather than walls, free facade, and roof garden.

facts.fact: The narrow, deep site and strict zoning rules shaped the design.
facts.quote: The design was constrained by the narrow (12 m (39 ft)) and deep (24 m (79 ft)) configuration of the site and by strict zoning codes, which specified the parapet height, conformance to the existing street wall, and even the placement of the balconies and bay windows.

facts.fact: Its all-glass facades, the same on both sides, were inspired by Chareau and Bijvoet's Maison de Verre, but add clear windows to the glass bricks.
facts.quote: Nevertheless, the architect's inventiveness is evident in the all-glass facades. Identical on both elevations, they were inspired by Pierre Chareau and Bernard Bijvoet's Maison de Verre, but Le Corbusier departed from Chareau's glass-brick-only prototype by the addition of transparent openings.

facts.fact: Le Corbusier's own apartment on the top two floors covers 240 square metres, arranged to avoid corridors and keep doors few.
facts.quote: The apartment that Le Corbusier built for his personal use on the top two floors extends over 240 m2 (2,600 sq ft). It is reached by stairs from the sixth floor, the last level served by the elevator. Rooms are arranged to eliminate corridors and minimize the number of doors.

facts.fact: His painting studio has a wall of stone and rough brick set against the concrete and glass.
facts.quote: The atelier that Le Corbusier used for his painting has a wall of stone and exposed rough brick that contrasts with the modern concrete and glass materials.

facts.fact: In 2016 it was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site with 16 other works by Le Corbusier.
facts.quote: In 2016 it was listed along with 16 other architectural works by Le Corbusier as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

facts.fact: Villa Schwob, also called Villa Turque, is a house in La Chaux-de-Fonds by Le Corbusier, commissioned in 1912 by the watchmaker Anatole Schwob and completed in 1917.
facts.quote: Villa Schwob also  Villa Turque is a house located in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland designed by noted architect Le Corbusier. It was commissioned in 1912 by the watchmaker Anatole Schwob, and completed in 1917.

facts.fact: Le Corbusier used regulating lines in its design for the first time.
facts.quote: Le Corbusier used the Regulating Lines design principle in this building for the first time.

facts.fact: It is the best known of his works in La Chaux-de-Fonds, finished before his move to Paris.
facts.quote: This is the most known of his creations in La Chaux-de-Fonds. The villa includes symbols, technical and aesthetic aspects. It was completed before his move to Paris.

facts.fact: Brickwork combined with concrete gives the house its oriental character.
facts.quote: The brick-work associated with concrete accentuates the oriental character of the house.

facts.fact: High walls enclose the house, which is fitted into its sloping plot.
facts.quote: Enclosed by high surrounding walls that ensure privacy, the house is integrated into its sloping plot.

facts.fact: It has three full storeys above a basement.
facts.quote: The structural composition spans three full primary stories in addition to a subterranean basement.

facts.fact: It became an official historical monument in 1995.
facts.quote: Recognizing its significant architectural value the house achieved formal designation as an official historical monument in 1995.

facts.fact: The French Communist Party headquarters is at Place du Colonel Fabien in Paris; its lead architect was Oscar Niemeyer.
facts.quote: The headquarters of the French Communist Party (French: siège du Parti communiste français) are located at 2 Place du Colonel Fabien in the 19th arrondissement of Paris. The lead architect was Oscar Niemeyer, who had previously designed many buildings for Brazil's new capital of Brasília.

facts.fact: It was designed in 1966, begun in 1968 and opened in 1971; the outer dome was finished only in 1980.
facts.quote: It was designed in 1966 and works began in 1968. The building was inaugurated in 1971; its external dome was not fully completed until 1980.

facts.fact: It is built of concrete with curves, and the dome where the National Council meets represents a pregnant woman, according to Niemeyer.
facts.quote: It was built in concrete and has curves. The dome, where the party's National Council sits, represents a pregnant woman according to the architect.

facts.fact: Niemeyer designed it while in exile in France during Brazil's military dictatorship.
facts.quote: Niemeyer, himself a communist, designed the building while living in exile in France during the military dictatorship in Brazil.

facts.fact: He worked with Paul Chemetov, Jean Deroche, José L. Pinho, Jean Prouvé and Jacques Tricot.
facts.quote: In designing the building, Niemeyer collaborated with Paul Chemetov, Jean Deroche, José L. Pinho, Jean Prouvé, and Jacques Tricot.

facts.fact: A Brutalist building, it was listed as a monument historique in 2007.
facts.quote: In 2007, the building  – a notable structure built in the style of Brutalist architecture  – was classed as a monument historique.

facts.fact: The university's new library, the Information, Communication and Media Centre (IKMZ), opened in 2004 and was designed by Herzog & de Meuron.
facts.quote: The new library was opened in the year 2004 and is called Informations-, Kommunikations- und Medienzentrum (IKMZ). It was designed by the famous architects Herzog & de Meuron.

facts.fact: Frank Lloyd Wright designed the house in the Usonian style for I. N. Hagan, owner of a local ice-cream firm, and his wife Bernardine.
facts.quote: Designed by the architect Frank Lloyd Wright in the Usonian style, the residence was built for Isaac Newton "I. N." Hagan, the owner of a local ice-cream firm, along with his wife, Bernardine.

facts.fact: It sits on the southern slope of a knoll above the Youghiogheny River gorge and is a National Historic Landmark.
facts.quote: It is built on the southern slope of a knoll known as Kentuck Knob, overlooking the Youghiogheny River gorge. The name of the house and knoll is derived from Little Kentuck, a hill in Fayette County named by an 18th-century settler who was planning to move to Kentucky. The house is a designated National Historic Landmark.

facts.fact: The house is built of redwood and local stone, with an overhanging copper roof and two terraces.
facts.quote: The house is made of redwood and locally-quarried stone, with an overhanging copper roof and two exterior terraces.

facts.fact: Two equal wings bend away from each other at 120 degrees and meet at a hexagonal core like a stone chimney.
facts.quote: The house has two wings (a living-room wing and bedroom wing), which bend away from each other at a 120-degree angle and are of equal length. The wings converge at a hexagonal core, which resembles a stone chimney.

facts.fact: The wings are laid out on a floor grid of equilateral triangles about 2.3 feet on a side.
facts.quote: These wings are built around a floor grid consisting of equilateral triangles measuring 2.3 feet (0.70 m) long on each side.

facts.fact: Like a passive solar house it faces west and south, reflecting Wright's belief that every room should get sunlight at some point in the day.
facts.quote: In a similar manner to a passive solar house, the building is oriented to the west and south, since the house primarily received natural light from these directions throughout the year. The orientation reflects Wright's belief that every room should be exposed to sunlight at some point throughout the day.

facts.fact: The bedroom wing is partly set into the hill.
facts.quote: The bedroom wing, extending to the northeast, is partly embedded into the adjacent knoll.

facts.fact: The eaves have hexagonal cut-outs that help ventilation and let patches of sunlight through.
facts.quote: The house has cantilevered eaves with hexagonal cutouts; there are 24 hexagonal cutouts on the southern elevation alone. These cutouts help with ventilation, and they also allow patches of sunlight to shine through the eaves, which otherwise create shadows.

facts.fact: The Humana Building is a 1985 skyscraper in downtown Louisville, Kentucky, built as the Humana Corporation's headquarters.
facts.quote: The Humana Building, also known as the Humana Tower, is a 1985 skyscraper in downtown Louisville, Kentucky, located at 500 West Main Street and is the former headquarters of the Humana Corporation.

facts.fact: The 26-storey tower was designed by Michael Graves and built from October 1982 to May 1985.
facts.quote: The 26-story structure is headquarters of the Humana Corporation, and was designed by the Driehaus Prize winner and New Classical architect Michael Graves. Construction began in October 1982 and was completed in May 1985.

facts.fact: Each side of the building is designed slightly differently, rising to a sloping pyramid form at the top.
facts.quote: Each side of the building is designed slightly differently, up to a sloping pyramid style for the upper few floors.

facts.fact: It is known for its outer walls of flat pink granite.
facts.quote: The building is also known for its exterior construction of flat pink granite.

facts.fact: The north loggia lines up with the old Main Street shopfronts, respecting the older downtown buildings.
facts.quote: The north facade's loggia is respectful of the older downtown architecture, being flush with the original Main Street storefronts.

facts.fact: The large curved part near the top is an open-air observation deck.
facts.quote: The large, curved portion towards the top of the building is an open-air observation deck.

facts.fact: It won an AIA National Honor Award in 1987, and Time named it one of the ten best buildings of the 1980s.
facts.quote: The American Institute of Architects awarded the Humana Building the National Honor Award in 1987. Time magazine listed it as one of the ten best buildings of the 1980s.

facts.fact: It is one of Graves's best-known postmodern buildings, with the Portland Building.
facts.quote: His postmodern buildings include the Portland Building in Portland, Oregon and the Humana Building in Louisville, Kentucky.

facts.fact: Maison Hermès, in Tokyo's Ginza district, is the French luxury brand's flagship store in Japan.
facts.quote: The Maison Hermès in the Ginza commercial district of Tokyo is the flagship store in Japan of the French luxury brand.

facts.fact: Built between 1998 and 2001, it was designed by Renzo Piano with Bohlin Cywinski Jackson and in collaboration with Takenaka Corporation.
facts.quote: Constructed between 1998 and 2001, it was designed by Renzo Piano assisted by Bohlin Cywinski Jackson of Berkeley, California and in collaboration with Takenaka Corporation.

facts.fact: It is also the corporate headquarters of Hermès in Japan.
facts.quote: The building is the flagship store and corporate headquarters of the French luxury-goods corporation, Hermès, in Japan.

facts.fact: The 6,000 square metre building holds workshops, offices, a shop, exhibition areas and multimedia rooms.
facts.quote: It is a 6,000 square metre (65,000 square feet) structure that houses workshops and offices, a shopping space, exhibition areas and multimedia quarters.

facts.fact: A recess splits the long facade in two, forming a courtyard that leads down to Ginza Station.
facts.quote: In addition to a roof garden at the top of the building, there is also a recess which divides the long facade into two, forming a courtyard that delivers an access to the Tokyo Metro's Ginza Station two levels below.

facts.fact: The facade is made of 13,000 glass blocks, each exactly 45 by 45 centimetres, on a building 44.55 metres high.
facts.quote: The building is highly geometrical; precisely 44.55 metres (146.2 ft) high, with a facade composed of 13,000 pieces of glass each exactly 45 by 45 centimetres (18 by 18 in).

facts.fact: The glass was made in Florence and set in Swiss-made supports, then assembled in Japan.
facts.quote: The panels of glass were made in Florence, Italy, and placed in supports made in Switzerland, for assembly in Japan.

facts.fact: Each piece of the facade can move four millimetres to resist earthquakes.
facts.quote: Each piece of the facade is designed to be able to move four millimetres (3⁄16 in) to resist earthquakes.

facts.fact: Lit at night, the building is meant to look like a "magic lantern".
facts.quote: When illuminated a night, the building is intended to resemble a "magic lantern".

facts.fact: The Haus des Rundfunks in Berlin is the world's oldest self-contained broadcasting centre.
facts.quote: The Haus des Rundfunks (transl. Broadcasting House), located in the Westend district of Berlin, the capital city of Germany, is the world's oldest self-contained broadcasting centre.

facts.fact: Hans Poelzig designed it in 1929 after winning a competition; three large studios sit in the middle, shielded from street noise by office wings around them.
facts.quote: Designed by Hans Poelzig in 1929 after he won an architectural competition, the building contains three large centrally located broadcasting spaces, which are shielded from street noise by the surrounding office wings.

facts.fact: Its plan is a triangle with two curved sides and a 150-metre straight facade clad in ceramic tiles; it opened on 22 January 1931.
facts.quote: The building, the ground plan of which is a triangle with two curved sides and a 150 m  long (490 ft) straight façade clad with ceramic tiles, was constructed between 1929 and 1930 and inaugurated on 22 January 1931 as the seat of the Reichs-Rundfunk-Gesellschaft.

facts.fact: Poelzig had almost no models to follow, but his layout of offices around the studios is still valid today.
facts.quote: At the time, Hans Poelzig had almost no examples to emulate but he developed ideas which are still valid today: the office and editorial rooms are located in the outer areas of the building, thereby surrounding the three large studio complexes.

facts.fact: The seats in the large studio were designed to absorb the same sound whether occupied or not.
facts.quote: The chairs in the large broadcasting space were specially designed so that seats had the same sound-absorbing qualities whether occupied or not.

facts.fact: In the smaller studio, a hundred wall panels could be flipped, one side absorbing sound and the other reflecting it.
facts.quote: In the smaller broadcasting room a hundred wall panels could be flipped. One side of the panels absorbed sound, the other reflected it.

facts.fact: Germany's first regular television service began here on 22 March 1935.
