facts.quote: On 22 March 1935 the first regular television service in Germany Fernsehsender Paul Nipkow was begun here, but moved to a separate building on nearby Theodor-Heuss-Platz in 1937.

facts.fact: The Research Institutes for Experimental Medicine in Berlin are commonly known as the Mouse Bunker, or Mäusebunker.
facts.quote: The Research Institutes for Experimental Medicine are a research facility in Berlin, Germany. This building is commonly known as Mouse Bunker, or Mäusebunker in German.

facts.fact: It was built for live animal testing, and animals were bred inside to keep conditions sterile and controlled.
facts.quote: This facility was built for the purpose of live animal testing. Animals for experimentation were bred in the facility too, to provide sterile conditions and a maximum amount of control.

facts.fact: Its original designers, Gerd and Magdalena Hänska, began the design between 1965 and 1967.
facts.quote: The Mouse Bunker's original designers are husband and wife Gerd Hänska and Magdalena Hänska. They started the design between 1965 and 1967.

facts.fact: Gerd Hänska and Kurt Schmersow did the detailed planning and construction between 1971 and 1981.
facts.quote: Detailed planning and construction was done by Gerd Hänska and Kurt Schmersow between 1971 and 1981.

facts.fact: Its sinister look and its use for animal testing made it unpopular with the public.
facts.quote: The building has been viewed as controversial from its very beginning. The sinister design and the use for animal testing were not popular with the general public.

facts.fact: Many international publications feature it as a leading example of brutalism in Germany.
facts.quote: Numerous international publications have featured Mouse Bunker as a prominent example of brutalist architecture in Germany.

facts.fact: After years of debate it was listed as a cultural heritage site in May 2023.
facts.quote: After a years long debate, the building was finally listed as a cultural heritage site in May 2023.

facts.fact: The church was built for German Catholics to honour the martyrs for freedom of belief and conscience of 1933–1945.
facts.quote: The church was built on behalf of the German Catholics to honour the Martyrs of Freedom of Belief and Conscience from the years 1933–1945.

facts.fact: It stands about 20 minutes' walk from Plötzensee Prison, where Nazi resisters were executed.
facts.quote: It is located 20 min of walk from the place of execution of Nazi resistants and opponents within the Plötzensee Prison, now the memorial Gedenkstätte Plötzensee.

facts.fact: Friedrich Ebert, Hermann Jünemann and Hans Schädel were commissioned to build it.
facts.quote: The episcopal ordinariate of the then Roman Catholic Diocese of Berlin commissioned Friedrich Ebert, Hermann Jünemann and Hans Schädel to build the church.

facts.fact: The cornerstone was laid in 1960 and the church was consecrated in 1963.
facts.quote: In 1960 Cardinal Julius Döpfner laid the cornerstone, and in 1963 he – together with Alfred Bengsch, then Catholic bishop of Berlin, and Louis-Marie-Fernand de Bazelaire, then Archbishop of Chambéry in France – consecrated the church.

facts.fact: The bell tower marks the entrance to a cobbled courtyard walled in black and grey basalt, with Stations of the Cross.
facts.quote: The campanile of Maria Regina Martyrum is a landmark at the entrance to the ceremonial courtyard, paved with cobblestone and surrounded by walls covered with slabs of black and grey basalt and showing figural Stations of the Cross.

facts.fact: The plain upper church has a flat ceiling and indirect lighting, and the building is seen as an outstanding union of church architecture and sculpture.
facts.quote: The sober interior of the upper church, covered by an even ceiling, impresses with its indirect illumination. The building is regarded an outstanding example of combining church architecture and sculpture.

facts.fact: The crypt is divided by a gold-coated concrete wall; the front part is a memorial to the martyrs.
facts.quote: The crypt, originally a single room, has been divided by a gold-coated wall of concrete. The front part is dedicated solely to the memory of the martyrs of that time, symbolised by three inscriptions.

facts.fact: Inside, a monumental fresco by Georg Meistermann covers the altar wall.
facts.quote: Inside on the altar wall there is a monumental fresco by Georg Meistermann.

facts.fact: In 1952 Alvar Aalto designed the Experimental House at Muuratsalo, in Central Finland, as a summer house for himself and his wife Elissa.
facts.quote: In 1952, he designed and built a summer cottage, the so-called Experimental House, for himself and his second wife, now Elissa Aalto, in Muuratsalo in Central Finland.

facts.fact: It stands on the shore of Lake Päijänne and was built in 1952–1954.
facts.quote: The experimental house of Muuratsalo is located on the shores of Lake Päijänne. It was built as a summer residence for Alvar and Elissa Aalto during 1952–1954, and used as the summer home by the Aalto family until 1994.

facts.fact: A partly open courtyard frames the landscape at its entrance and blurs inside and outside.
facts.quote: The house is enclosed by a provisional courtyard space which, when looking outward, frames the landscape within its entrance. This partial enclosure mediates the space, creating a distinction between interior and exterior, open and closed form.

facts.fact: Its walls mix different reclaimed bricks and bricklaying patterns.
facts.quote: The facade uses a mix of different styles of reclaimed bricks and bricklaying arrangements.

facts.fact: Aalto saw it as a studio and test site, where untried ideas could be tried out close to nature.
facts.quote: Aalto described this group of buildings as a combination of an architect's studio and an experimental centre, in which one could also carry out experiments that are not yet sufficiently well developed to be tried out in practice and where the proximity of nature may offer inspiration for both form and structure.

facts.fact: It belongs to Aalto's red-brick period, which began with Baker House at MIT.
facts.quote: Originally used in Baker House to signify the Ivy League university tradition, Aalto went on to use it in a number of key buildings after his return to Finland, most notably in several of the buildings in the new Helsinki University of Technology campus (starting in 1950), Säynätsalo Town Hall (1952), Helsinki Pensions Institute (1954), Helsinki House of Culture (1958), as well as in his own summer house, the Experimental House in Muuratsalo (1957).

facts.fact: The Alvar Aalto Museum now owns the house.
facts.quote: Since then, the house has been acquired by the museum.

facts.fact: Rødovre Town Hall, west of Copenhagen, was designed by Arne Jacobsen and completed in 1956.
facts.quote: Rødovre Town Hall (Danish: Rødovre Rådhus) is located at the centre of Rødovre, a municipality some 9 km (5 mi) to the west of Copenhagen's city centre. Completed in 1956, it was designed by the Danish architect Arne Jacobsen.

facts.fact: It was inspired by Eero Saarinen's General Motors Technical Center near Detroit.
facts.quote: A fine example of the international architecture trends of the 1950s, it was inspired by the General Motors Technical Center to the north of Detroit.

facts.fact: It has two wings joined by a glass corridor.
facts.quote: The complex consists of two wings connected by a glass corridor.

facts.fact: The three-storey office wing, 91 metres long, is built of pillars, precast beams and floor slabs.
facts.quote: The three-storey office wing, 91 m long and 14 m wide, is constructed of pillars, precast crossbeams and floor slabs.

facts.fact: Its load-bearing end walls are clad in dark stone, and the long curtain walls are grey glass in metal frames.
facts.quote: The loadbearing gable walls are clad in dark stone while the longitudinal curtain walls consist of grey glass set in metal frames with stainless steel trimmings.

facts.fact: The single-storey council chamber has stone-clad long sides and fully glazed ends; Jacobsen also designed its interior and furniture.
facts.quote: Its longitudinal facades are clad in dark stone while the gables are continuous windows. The lofty council chamber is a rectangular room in which the interior and furnishings were also designed by Jacobsen.

facts.fact: Its central staircase hangs from the roof on orange-red steel rods, with steel steps only a few millimetres thick.
facts.quote: The building is also noted for its central staircase, suspended from the roof on orange-red steel rods. The sides are cut from 5 cm steel plate, painted a dark grey; the steps, only a few millimeters thick, are stainless steel with a rubber coating on the upper side for better grip.

facts.fact: Completed in 1950, the house was designed by Bengt Edman and Lennart Holm for the Pharmacia head Elis Göth, and is a listed building.
facts.quote: Completed in 1950, the home is listed as having a special architectural interest in Sweden (byggnadsminne). Architects Bengt Edman and Lennart Holm designed it as the residence of Pharmacia head Elis Göth.

facts.fact: It is believed to be the source of the word brutalism.
facts.quote: The building has significance in international architectural history as the believed source of the term brutalism.

facts.fact: The term is thought to have been coined in 1950 by Hans Asplund in a joking remark about the house.
facts.quote: It is believed to have been coined in 1950 by Swedish architect Hans Asplund in a facetious comment about Villa Göth.

facts.fact: It has two floors and a basement and is built of dark brick.
facts.quote: Villa Göth has two floors and a basement and is built in dark brick.

facts.fact: Visible I-beams over the windows show openly how it is built.
facts.quote: The visible I-beams over the window sections in the front and rear of the building are an example of how the choice of materials is openly displayed in the house.

facts.fact: The ceilings show the board pattern of the concrete formwork, and some inside walls are the same dark brick as outside.
facts.quote: The tongue-and-groove pattern of the boards used to build the forms for the poured concrete is visible in the ceilings. Several interior walls are of the same dark brick as the exterior.

facts.fact: The first-floor bathrooms are raw concrete shaped like Alvar Aalto's Aalto Vase.
facts.quote: The bathrooms on the first floor are formed of raw concrete (béton brut) in the form of Alvar Aalto's famous Aalto Vase.

facts.fact: It was listed as historically significant on 3 March 1995.
facts.quote: This well-preserved and culturally significant house was listed as historically significant by the Uppsala county administrative board on March 3, 1995.

facts.fact: Monte Amiata Housing is a housing complex in Milan's Gallaratese district, designed by Carlo Aymonino and Aldo Rossi in the late 1960s.
facts.quote: Monte Amiata Housing is a residential complex in the Gallaratese district of Milan, Italy, designed by architects Carlo Aymonino and Aldo Rossi in the late 1960s.

facts.fact: It is nicknamed the "Red Dinosaur" for its red colour and unusual design.
facts.quote: It is sometimes referred to as the "Red Dinosaur" in reference both to the reddish color of the buildings and the oddity of their design.

facts.fact: It is seen as a key example of Aymonino's idea of the city as a varied, intricate texture, known as "fragmentism".
facts.quote: The project is well known in the international architecture community, and regarded as one of those that better represent Aymonino's vision of the city as a turbulent, intricate, and varied texture, a paradigm that is known as "fragmentism".

facts.fact: Five red buildings are grouped around a yellow open-air theatre and two small triangular squares.
facts.quote: The complex comprises five red buildings: two eight-stories slabs, a long three-stories building, another three-stories slab, and an interconnecting structure; these are grouped around a central area with a yellow, open-air theater, and two smaller triangular plazas.

facts.fact: Passages, decks, lifts, balconies, terraces and bridges link the buildings and give many walking routes.
facts.quote: The complexity of the skyline is enriched by a number of passages, decks, elevators, balconies, terraces and bridges connecting the buildings with each other and providing for a great variety of pedestrian walking paths.

facts.fact: It was conceived as a utopian small city within the city.
facts.quote: The complex was conceived as an utopian micro-city within the city, and based on Aymonino and Rossi's vision, emphasizing the interplay between housing blocks and their urban context.

facts.fact: The architects named Le Corbusier's Unité d'Habitation as a main source, aiming to improve on it.
facts.quote: Aymonino and Rossi explicitly mentioned the Unité d'Habitation in Marseille as one of their main sources of inspiration, although their intent was to improve on Le Corbusier's model.

facts.fact: Rossi drew on Giorgio de Chirico's paintings for one of the five buildings, the smaller slab.
facts.quote: Rossi also took inspiration from Giorgio de Chirico's paintings when designing one of the five buildings, the smaller slab.

facts.fact: Josep Maria Jujol built the Torre de la Creu in Sant Joan Despí, Province of Barcelona, in 1913–1916.
